one_liner: Google's ML framework; with XLA plus mixed precision (NVIDIA's 2020 TF 1.15 build) it out-trained NGC PyTorch on ResNet-50 and BERT-base.
what_it_does: TensorFlow is an end-to-end machine-learning platform: a C++ runtime with GPU/CPU kernels, graph and eager execution, automatic differentiation, tf.data input pipelines, distributed training and the XLA compiler, exposed through stable Python and C++ APIs. It is not a drop-in for PyTorch: models, training loops and checkpoints have to be written for TensorFlow/Keras. The catalogued result is training throughput of NVIDIA's DeepLearningExamples models run in NVIDIA's NGC TensorFlow 1.15.2 container, not a kernel or library you call from your own code.
how_it_is_fast: The lead comes from the XLA JIT compiler (--use_xla), which fuses graph ops into fewer, larger GPU kernels: inside the same suite XLA alone lifts ResNet-50 AMP from 945.18 to 1198.55 img/s on one V100 (about 1.27x) and BERT-base AMP from 183.25 to 422.53 sentences/s (about 2.3x, both derived from page data). Mixed precision comes from NVIDIA's automatic-mixed-precision graph rewrite (--use_tf_amp) with a static loss scale of 128; multi-GPU scaling uses Horovod over NCCL and InfiniBand, and images are decoded on the GPU by DALI (nvJPEG 'mixed' decoder).
when_to_use: You already train in TensorFlow/Keras on NVIDIA GPUs and can turn on XLA (jit_compile) and mixed precision: in this suite those two switches are what put TensorFlow ahead.
CNN training of ResNet-50 class models with AMP on V100-class GPUs and a GPU-side input pipeline (DALI or similar), from 1 GPU to 4 nodes x 8 GPUs.
BERT-base style pretraining with AMP only if XLA is enabled; then TensorFlow led NGC PyTorch by 1-13% at the largest per-GPU batch (96).
Deployments that need a C++ runtime and a maintained, Apache-2.0 framework with official wheels for Linux x86-64/aarch64, macOS arm64 and Windows.
when_not_to_use: FP32 training: in the same report PyTorch is faster on ResNet-50 at every scale (NGC PyTorch 10917.09 vs NGC TensorFlow 9514.64 img/s on 32 GPUs) and on BERT-base at batch 32.

Transformer training without XLA: NGC TensorFlow BERT-base AMP was about 2.4x slower than NGC PyTorch on one GPU (183.25 vs 444.51 sentences/s), and stock TensorFlow 2.3.0 BERT AMP was about 2.5x slower on 32 GPUs (4168.79 vs 10349.12).
Choosing on raw ResNet-50 throughput alone: NGC MXNet (1393.87 vs 1198.55 img/s on one GPU) and OneFlow beat TensorFlow-with-XLA in the same table.

Expecting the 2020 numbers to carry over: the winning build is TensorFlow 1.15.2 in the NGC 20.03 container; the maintained line is 2.x (2.21.0, March 2026) and stock TF 2.3.0 lost to NGC PyTorch at 16 and 32 GPUs.
C/C++ embedding from prebuilt binaries: TensorFlow stopped publishing libtensorflow packages in 2.19 (the release notes say to unpack it from the PyPI wheel), otherwise you build with Bazel.

integration.form: pip wheel (Python) or shared library (libtensorflow / libtensorflow_cc) built from source with Bazel
integration.dependencies: Bazel 7.7.0 for source builds; hermetic CUDA 12.5.1 and cuDNN 9.10.0 by default for GPU builds (CUDA 13 config available); Horovod, NCCL and DALI were added separately in the benchmarked NGC setup
integration.min_toolchain: C++17 (.bazelrc sets -std=c++17 on all platforms); Python >= 3.10 for TensorFlow 2.21
integration.platforms: Linux x86-64 and aarch64, macOS arm64, Windows x86-64 (PyPI wheels); NVIDIA GPUs via CUDA; the benchmark ran on Tesla V100-SXM2-16GB
integration.thread_safety: not documented in the pages read

gotchas: Harness flaw in the ResNet-50 AMP comparison: TensorFlow reads TFRecords through DALI with GPU nvJPEG decoding and GPU resize (NVIDIA data_utils passes dali_cpu=False), while DLPerf's NGC PyTorch script hard-codes --data-backend dali-cpu, so PyTorch decodes JPEGs and runs RandomResizedCrop on the host Xeon Gold 5118 CPUs (NVIDIA's README does recommend dali-cpu for DGX-1).

Harness flaw: TensorFlow ran AMP with --use_static_loss_scaling --loss_scale=128, PyTorch with --dynamic-loss-scale; DLPerf's own static-loss-scale PyTorch run is 827.86 and 6446.74 img/s on 1 and 8 GPUs, not the reported 802.9 and 6154.66, which cuts TensorFlow's 1.49x and 1.40x leads to about 1.45x and 1.33x. NVIDIA's own READMEs still put TensorFlow 20.03 ahead (AMP 1099.55 img/s, 1217.90 with XLA, vs PyTorch AMP 856.52 img/s on one V100 16GB), so the ordering holds while the margin is inflated.

Metric mismatch: TensorFlow ResNet-50 throughput is the arithmetic mean of rank 0's per-step imgs_per_sec (extract_tensorflow_logs.py, 100 steps after a 20-step warmup), while PyTorch's comes from elapsed time over the same window (extract_pytorch_logs_time.py); a mean of rates is never below the time-based figure, and DLPerf says the two methods differ slightly. Batch sizes also differ (TensorFlow 224 after OOM at 256 vs PyTorch 256), which works against TensorFlow.

XLA and the regular kernels can disagree: the 2.22 release notes fix jit_compile=True silently accepting integer inputs for Reciprocal/Inv and segfaulting in non_max_suppression on empty boxes, so validate numerics when enabling XLA.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Choose TensorFlow over PyTorch only when you can run it with XLA plus AMP, since the PyTorch entry's FP32 and non-XLA rows go the other way. For raw ResNet-50 throughput in this same suite, MXNet (NGC build) and OneFlow were faster. CNTK beat TensorFlow 1.2 on LSTMs, and Flashlight beat TensorFlow 2.4, so only reach for TensorFlow on speed when its XLA path applies.
verified_claims_summary: OneFlow's DLPerf report (October 2020; 4 nodes x 8 Tesla V100-SXM2-16GB, Xeon Gold 5118, CUDA 10.2, InfiniBand EDR; median of 5-6 runs, 100 steps after 20 warmup) measured NGC TensorFlow 1.15.2 with XLA and AMP at 1198.55 vs 802.9 img/s for NGC PyTorch 1.5.0a0 on ResNet-50 v1.5 with one GPU and 29171.69 vs 22551.16 on 32 GPUs (about 1.49x and 1.29x, derived from page data). On BERT-base AMP at batch 96 the figures were 468.10 vs 462.35 and 11650.0 vs 10349.12 sentences/s (about 1.01x and 1.13x); the data pipelines and loss scaling differed between the two frameworks, and container compiler flags are not stated.
status_note: Actively maintained under Apache-2.0 (200.9k stars, 2.21.0 released 2026-03-06, 2.22.0rc0 on 2026-09-22), but the benchmarked winner is a 2020 NVIDIA build of TensorFlow 1.15. XLA is developed as OpenXLA and copied into third_party/xla, and tf.lite is moving out to LiteRT.
